blocks.title: Chemical bond
blocks.text: A chemical bond is the force that holds together two or more atoms, molecules or ions. The properties of a substance depend on the type of chemical bond between its atoms.

The term chemical bond includes ionic, covalent, dative and metallic bonds as well as intermolecular forces, the van der Waals forces; being weak, the van der Waals forces are usually not called pure chemical bonds. This chapter discusses the types of bond in the light of electronegativity and its effect on the nature of bonding, dipole moment and polarity; then the modern bonding theories, VSEPR, VBT, hybridization and MOT; then the intermolecular forces; and finally a comparison of chemical bonds and intermolecular forces in terms of bond energies. Sodium chloride has an ionic bond and is a solid, while water is a covalent compound and a liquid.

The Lewis concept of bonding gives a simple explanation of the formation of all types of bond. According to this theory, atoms make bonds to complete their outermost shells and so have a noble-gas-like configuration, which is mostly attained by forming an octet in the valence shell.

blocks.alt: Top row: sodium hands one electron to chlorine, two chlorine atoms share a pair, and notes on the dative bonds in H3O+, CO and O3. Bottom row: the Lewis structure of the sulfate ion with two double and two single bonds, sulfur's 3s 3p 3d boxes before and after one electron moves to 3d, and the tri-iodide ion with three lone pairs on the central iodine.
blocks.caption: Ionic, covalent and dative bonds by the Lewis concept, and expanded octets in sulfate and tri-iodide (original diagram after Figures 3.1 to 3.3 and the printed Lewis structures).
blocks.long_description: Sodium, with low ionization energy, gives its single outer electron to chlorine, which has high electron affinity; the ions Na+ and Cl- then attract each other. Two chlorine atoms, equally electronegative, share one pair and each counts eight. In a dative bond one atom supplies both electrons: oxygen's lone pair to a proton in H3O+, oxygen's lone pair to carbon in CO, and a central oxygen's pair to a third oxygen in ozone. In the sulfate ion the sulfur atom has twelve valence electrons, four beyond the octet, because one 3p electron can move into an empty 3d orbital; the central iodine of I3- has ten. Period 2 atoms have no d orbitals and cannot expand.
